title: The mosque community

lines: A WEEKEND SCHOOL IN THE BASEMENT.
ALL OF IT IS THE MOSQUE.
cards: Ask who runs a mosque, and the quick answer is the imam. Then look on a Saturday morning at a mosque in the suburbs.

In the basement, kids at folding tables learn the Arabic letters, and one is drawing a dinosaur in the margin. Upstairs, the committee argues politely about whether the new carpet should be green or blue.
In the kitchen, two aunties plan next month's iftar. Out front, a man in a reflective vest sorts out the parking. Nobody here is praying right now.
And all of it is the mosque.

teach.h: THE EARTH IS A PLACE OF PRAYER.
teach.b: Begin with a surprise from al-Bukhari.

The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, listed things given to him, and one was this, in paraphrase: the earth has been made for me a place of prayer and a means of purification, so wherever the time of prayer reaches you, pray.
Any clean patch of ground will do. Then why build one? Look at the Prophet's mosque in Madinah.
Al-Bukhari reports that when it was built, the Prophet carried building materials alongside his companions. Before there was a committee or a carpet, there were people hauling things together.

Then the person nobody noticed. Al-Bukhari tells of someone who used to sweep the mosque; the narrator isn't sure whether it was a man or a woman. When the sweeper died, people didn't think to tell the Prophet.
Later he asked about the sweeper and heard. He said, in paraphrase: why didn't you tell me? Show me the grave.
And he went and prayed there.
The sweeper was missed by name.

teach.h: A HALL AND EVERYONE AROUND IT.
teach.b: Today, a mosque is often a prayer hall plus everything around it: an imam who leads and teaches, a board that pays the bills, volunteers for the weekend school, the funeral committee, the iftar kitchen, the food pantry.
The prayer could happen anywhere. What the building gathers is people, and people are how a stranger in town finds a meal, a funeral prayer, a teacher for their kid.

how: Mosques are often run by volunteer boards and committees alongside an imam, and host weekend schools for children, iftars in Ramadan, funeral services, food drives and open days, with members volunteering for cleaning, teaching, cooking and parking.

the people who keep a mosque running

games.q: the person who used to sweep the mosque has died, and nobody told the Prophet. when he finds out, what does he do?
o: lets it go; it was only the sweeper.
asks to be shown the grave, and prays there.

games.why: he asked why they hadn't told him, asked to be shown the grave, and prayed there. the sweeper was missed by name.

practice: Picture the scene again, the basement school, the kitchen, the parking vest, the broom, and ask which job you could do: reading to kids, stacking chairs, washing up after an iftar, driving someone older to Friday prayer.
If you're not Muslim, some mosques welcome help with open days, food drives and interfaith meals. Let one small job come clear, and if you pray, ask that it be accepted.

wordCard.voice: The mosque community. The people around the prayer hall: imam, board, teachers, cooks, sweepers, volunteers. The building gathers them; they make it a mosque. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a mosque, a place of prayer.

carryVoice: Your line: the mosque is people. Any clean ground holds a prayer; people make a mosque. Until tomorrow.
